paper.title: Risk of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest among sepsis survivors in Taiwan: analysis of a nationwide population-based cohort
paper.authors: Hsu WT, Sherrod CF, Tehrani B, Papaila A, Porta L, Hsu TC, Sheng WH, Lee CC.

study.population: Patients with sepsis discharged from hospitals in Taiwan between 2000 and 2013, followed for up to 1 year post-discharge.

exposure.name: Sepsis
exposure.definition: Sepsis identified using ICD-9-CM codes for sepsis combined with acute organ dysfunction according to Martin criteria and Sepsis-3 definition.

outcome.name: Out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA)
outcome.definition: OHCA identified by ICD-9-CM codes 427.5, 798, or procedure code 99.60 within 365 days of discharge.

nodes.label: Age
nodes.snippet: matched according to admission date, 5-year age group

nodes.label: Charlson Comorbidity Score
nodes.snippet: matched according to Charlson Comorbidity Score quartile

missing_confounders.label: Renal dysfunction
missing_confounders.rationale: Chronic kidney disease increases susceptibility to sepsis and independently predisposes to arrhythmic cardiac arrest via electrolyte shifts and uremic cardiomyopathy.

missing_confounders.label: QT‑prolonging medication use
missing_confounders.rationale: Patients with sepsis often receive antibiotics (e.g., macrolides, fluoroquinolones) or antipsychotics that prolong QT interval, raising OHCA risk; prescribing patterns also correlate with sepsis severity.

missing_confounders.label: Prior arrhythmia / heart failure severity
missing_confounders.rationale: A history of ventricular arrhythmias or severe heart failure raises both the likelihood of developing sepsis (due to reduced reserve) and the risk of OHCA after discharge.

bias_risks.explanation: The cohort includes only patients who survived sepsis hospitalization to discharge; those who died in-hospital are excluded, potentially inflating the observed post‑discharge OHCA risk among survivors.
Sepsis and OHCA are identified solely from ICD‑9‑CM codes; misclassification (e.g., coding errors, lack of clinical confirmation) can bias the hazard ratio toward or away from the null.
Important severity markers (lactate, SOFA, ICU admission) and medication exposures were not adjusted for, leaving open the possibility that sicker sepsis patients drive the OHCA association.
Propensity‑score matching on variables that may be consequences of sepsis (e.g., infection source, septic shock) can induce collider bias, distorting the sepsis–OHCA relationship.
Although the NHIRD is near‑complete, emigration or death outside the health system could lead to censoring that differs by sepsis status, potentially biasing estimates.

critique.overall_assessment: The study provides evidence of an association between sepsis hospitalization and increased risk of out‑of‑hospital cardiac arrest up to one year later, but the causal interpretation is weakened by potential immortal time bias, measurement error, and residual confounding from unmeasured sepsis severity and medication exposures. While adjustment for demographics, comorbidities, and infection characteristics reduces confounding, important prognostic factors remain uncontrolled. Consequently, the observed hazard ratios should be viewed as suggestive rather than definitive proof of a causal effect.
